questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three GBM assumptions this lesson audits?
options: Log-returns are i.i.d. normal
Volatility is constant over the modeled horizon
The drift is a single constant estimable from historical averages
The asset's price must be below $1,000
questions.explain: The lesson audits three specific GBM assumptions: i.i.d. normal log-returns, constant volatility, and a stable, estimable drift. There is no assumption in GBM about an absolute price ceiling.

questions.q: In the fat-tails comparison code, the fat-tailed (Student's t) returns show excess kurtosis of about +8.5 while the GBM-normal returns show excess kurtosis near 0. What does this demonstrate?
options: The fat-tailed sample has lower volatility than the normal sample

The fat-tailed distribution produces large moves (extreme returns) far more often than a normal distribution would, holding volatility fixed — a direct, quantified version of the 'fat tails' critique of GBM
Excess kurtosis near 0 means the normal sample has fatter tails
The two samples are statistically identical
questions.explain: Excess kurtosis measures tail weight relative to the normal distribution (0 is the normal benchmark); the fat-tailed sample's much higher excess kurtosis of about 8.5 numerically confirms it produces extreme moves more frequently than GBM's normal log-return assumption allows.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Lesson 40's noisy drift estimate (mu_hat ~0.033 vs true 0.08) should be reported honestly rather than omitted from a presentation of the project?
options: Because reporting unflattering results is required by convention, regardless of insight
Because volunteering and explaining a real limitation demonstrates the kind of self-aware quantitative judgment that interviewers specifically look for, beyond just 'the code ran'
Because the true mu value is actually unknowable in any model
Because reporting it makes the Monte Carlo simulation more accurate
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames volunteering limitation #3 (noisy drift estimation) as exactly the kind of judgment that separates someone who merely ran the code from someone who understands what the model does and doesn't do well — a distinction interviewers are testing for.

questions.q: What is the suggested four-part structure for presenting this capstone project?
options: Code, data, output, conclusion
Problem, method, results (including unflattering ones), limitations and extensions
Introduction, literature review, abstract, references
Hypothesis, experiment, p-value, publication
questions.explain: The lesson recommends structuring the presentation as: state the problem and why GBM was chosen, name the exact methods (MLE calibration, Monte Carlo simulation), report results honestly including the noisy drift estimate, and name limitations with their natural extensions.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what are the natural extensions that address GBM's three audited limitations (fat tails, volatility clustering, noisy drift)?
options: Ignore all three, since GBM is already a perfect model

A fat-tailed or jump-diffusion return model for fat tails, a GARCH-style model for volatility clustering, and either more data, a Bayesian prior, or de-emphasizing direction-driven forecasts for the noisy drift
Switching entirely to linear regression
Using a larger initial price S_0
questions.explain: The lesson names Student's t or jump-diffusion models as the extension for fat tails, GARCH for volatility clustering, and longer data history, a Bayesian prior on mu, or relying more on volatility-driven (rather than direction-driven) uses of the model as responses to noisy drift estimation.
